claim: The visual system samples attended information rhythmically.
source: It has been suggested that the visual system samples attended information rhythmically.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on rhythmic visual sampling.

claim: Rhythmic visual sampling is mediated by low-frequency intrinsic brain oscillations.
source: Recent work has suggested that to manage the limited capacity problem, the visual system samples the attended information in a rhythmic fashion, mediated by low-frequency intrinsic brain oscillations (Chota et al., 2022; Dugué et al., 2015; Fiebelkorn et al., 2013; Fiebelkorn et al., 2018; Fiebelkorn and Kastner, 2019; Helfrich et al., 2018; Michel et al., 2022; Re et al., 2019; VanRullen, 2013; Zalta et al., 2020).
evidence: Multiple citations support this claim about the mechanism of rhythmic sampling.

claim: When a stimulus occurs during the high excitability phase of a low-frequency brain oscillation, behavioral performance tends to be better than average.
source: When a stimulus occurs during the high excitability phase, behavioral performance tends to be better than average; conversely, if the stimulus occurs during the low excitability phase, performance is generally worse than average (Lakatos et al., 2008; VanRullen, 2013).
evidence: Citations to prior studies support this claim about phase-dependent performance.

claim: When attending to one object in isolation, the frequency of rhythmic sampling tends to be around 8 Hz.
source: When attending to one object in isolation, the frequency of rhythmic sampling tends to be in the high theta or low alpha frequency range, i.e., around 8 Hz (Fiebelkorn et al., 2013; Senoussi et al., 2019; van der Werf et al., 2023).
evidence: Citations to prior studies support this specific frequency claim.

claim: When attention is directed to multiple objects, the brain samples the objects in a serial fashion rather than simultaneously.
source: When attention is directed to multiple objects in the environment, it has been suggested that rather than sampling all the objects simultaneously, the brain samples the objects in a serial fashion (Cohen et al., 1990; Wyart et al., 2012).
evidence: Citations support this claim about serial sampling of multiple objects.

claim: Serial sampling of multiple objects leads to a slower rhythmic sampling frequency around 4 Hz.
source: This would then lead to a slower rhythmic sampling of any given object, in the low range of the theta frequency band, i.e., around 4 Hz (Thigpen et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation supports this claim about reduced sampling frequency with multiple objects.

claim: When participants attend to both cued and uncued visual hemifields, the rhythmic detection rate for targets in a given hemifield decreases from 8 Hz to 4 Hz.
source: For example, when participants were cued to attend one visual hemifield but were asked to detect the appearance of a weak stimulus in either the cued or the uncued visual hemifield, the rhythmic detection rate for the target appearing in a given visual hemifield decreased from 8 Hz to 4 Hz (Chota et al., 2022; Fiebelkorn et al., 2013; VanRullen, 2013).
evidence: Citations to prior studies support this specific finding about frequency reduction.

claim: The visual system samples cued and uncued visual hemifields in a serial, alternating fashion with a 180-degree relative phase.
source: Interestingly, when the detection rate functions of the cued and uncued targets were compared, a 180-degree relative phase was apparent, suggesting that the visual system indeed sampled the two visual hemifields in a serial, alternating fashion (Fiebelkorn et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2024).
evidence: Citations support this claim about alternating sampling with specific phase relationship.

claim: In the presence of a distractor, the processing of the target is negatively impacted, leading to reduced task performance.
source: It is well established that in the presence of a distractor, the processing of the target is negatively impacted, leading to reduced task performance (Lavie, 2005; Murphy et al., 2016).
evidence: Citations support this established finding about distractor effects.

claim: Distractors are processed in the brain despite needing to be suppressed by the executive control system.
source: This implies that the distractor, despite the need for it to be suppressed by the brain's executive control system (Kastner et al., 1998; Kastner et al., 1999; Kastner and Pinsk, 2004; Seidl et al., 2012; Kastner and Ungerleider, 2000), is nevertheless processed in the brain, and the competition between the target and the distractor at the neural representational level causes the detriment in behavioral performance.
evidence: Citations support this claim about distractor processing and suppression.

claim: The moving dots in the experiment were flickered at 4.29 Hz.
source: The moving dots were flickered at 4.29 Hz, whereas the IAPS pictures were flickered at 6 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: The IAPS pictures in the experiment were flickered at 6 Hz.
source: The moving dots were flickered at 4.29 Hz, whereas the IAPS pictures were flickered at 6 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Each trial in the experiment lasted approximately 12 seconds.
source: The target and the distractor were flickered at two different frequencies for an extended duration of ~12 s.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: EEG data were collected from 27 subjects performing a sustained attention task.
source: EEG data were collected from 27 subjects performing a sustained attention task.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample.

claim: Each participant performed 84 trials.
source: Each participant performed 84 trials.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: The overall coherent motion detection accuracy was 55.73% ± 2.94%.
source: The overall coherent motion detection accuracy was 55.73% ± 2.94%, with that for pleasant, neutral, and unpleasant trials being 55.67% ± 2.76%, 55.03% ± 3.10%, and 56.48% ± 3.61%, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data from the experiment.

claim: There was no significant difference in behavioral performance between the three types of trials (pleasant, neutral, unpleasant).
source: A one-way ANOVA found no significant difference in behavioral performance between the three types of trials (F2, 78 = 0.053, p=0.949), suggesting that the three types of distractors exerted similar distracting influence on the detection of coherent motion, irrespective of their emotional significance.
evidence: Statistical test results support this claim.

claim: The three types of distractors exerted similar distracting influence on the detection of coherent motion, irrespective of their emotional significance.
source: A one-way ANOVA found no significant difference in behavioral performance between the three types of trials (F2, 78 = 0.053, p=0.949), suggesting that the three types of distractors exerted similar distracting influence on the detection of coherent motion, irrespective of their emotional significance.
evidence: This is inferred from the statistical test showing no difference between conditions.

claim: Spectral peaks corresponding to the flicker frequencies of 4.29 Hz (target) and 6 Hz (distractor) are clearly seen in the Fourier spectrum of the grand average SSVEP at Oz.
source: From Figure 2B, spectral peaks corresponding to the flicker frequencies of 4.29 Hz (target) and 6 Hz (distractor) are clearly seen.
evidence: This is directly observed in the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The 4.29 Hz amplitude was significantly greater than the 6 Hz amplitude.
source: Averaging target amplitude and distractor amplitude across all electrodes, the 4.29 Hz amplitude was significantly greater than the 6 Hz amplitude (p=2.6 × 10–4); see Figure 2C.
evidence: Statistical comparison of amplitudes supports this claim.

claim: The strongest SSVEP response for both target and distractor frequencies was concentrated in the occipital channels.
source: SSVEP amplitude topographies for target and distractor in Figure 2D showed that the strongest response for both frequencies was concentrated in the occipital channels.
evidence: Topographical analysis shown in Figure 2D supports this claim.

claim: There was no correlation between target SSVEP amplitude and task performance.
source: Across participants, there was no correlation between target SSVEP amplitude and task performance (p=0.7536); see Figure 2E, left.
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis supports this claim.

claim: The SSVEP amplitude of the distractor has a slight negative correlation with task performance, but it is not statistically significant.
source: The SSVEP amplitude of the distractor has a slight negative correlation with task performance, indicating that the stronger the distractor processing, the worse the performance, but it is not statistically significant (p=0.1896).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis supports this claim.

claim: IAPS pictures from different emotion categories evoke distinct spatial patterns in EEG which can be decoded using machine-learning-based MVPA methods.
source: Our previous work has shown that IAPS pictures from different emotion categories evoke distinct spatial patterns in EEG which can be decoded using machine-learning-based MVPA methods (Bo et al., 2022).
evidence: Citation to prior work supports this claim.

claim: The pairwise decoding accuracy for pleasant vs neutral was 57.86% ± 9.86%, which was significantly above the chance level of 50%.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, for pleasant vs neutral, unpleasant vs neutral, and unpleasant vs neutral, the pairwise decoding accuracy was 57.86% ± 9.86%, 55.14% ± 8.17%, and 59.45% ± 9.73%, respectively, which were all significantly above the chance level of 50% at p=3.2 × 10–4, p=3.0 × 10–3, and p=3.0 × 10–5, respectively.
evidence: Statistical test results and Figure 3A support this claim.

claim: The pairwise decoding accuracy for unpleasant vs neutral was 55.14% ± 8.17%, which was significantly above the chance level of 50%.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, for pleasant vs neutral, unpleasant vs neutral, and unpleasant vs neutral, the pairwise decoding accuracy was 57.86% ± 9.86%, 55.14% ± 8.17%, and 59.45% ± 9.73%, respectively, which were all significantly above the chance level of 50% at p=3.2 × 10–4, p=3.0 × 10–3, and p=3.0 × 10–5, respectively.
evidence: Statistical test results and Figure 3A support this claim.

claim: The pairwise decoding accuracy for pleasant vs unpleasant was 59.45% ± 9.73%, which was significantly above the chance level of 50%.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, for pleasant vs neutral, unpleasant vs neutral, and unpleasant vs neutral, the pairwise decoding accuracy was 57.86% ± 9.86%, 55.14% ± 8.17%, and 59.45% ± 9.73%, respectively, which were all significantly above the chance level of 50% at p=3.2 × 10–4, p=3.0 × 10–3, and p=3.0 × 10–5, respectively.
evidence: Statistical test results and Figure 3A support this claim.

claim: The three-way decoding accuracy was 41.09% ± 6.25%, which is significantly above chance level of 33.33%.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, the three-way decoding accuracy was found to be 41.09% ± 6.25%, which is again significantly above chance level of 33.33% at p=3.9 × 10–7.
evidence: Statistical test results and Figure 3B support this claim.

claim: No correlation was found between distractor decoding accuracy and task performance.
source: Similar to distractor SSVEP amplitude, no correlation was found between distractor decoding accuracy and task performance; see Figure 3C.
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis and Figure 3C support this claim.

claim: Distractor decoding accuracy and distractor amplitude are independent indices of distractor processing.
source: Also, in order to verify that the distractor decoding accuracy and the distractor amplitude were independent indices of distractor processing, we correlated the two across participants. As Figure 3D shows, no correlation was found, suggesting that the two quantities provided complementary characterization of distractor processing (also see Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: Lack of correlation between the two measures supports their independence.

claim: The attended target was sampled rhythmically with a sampling frequency at approximately 1 Hz.
source: Across all participants, the averaged Fourier spectrum is shown in Figure 4Aii, where the frequency of the spectral peak was found to be 1.08±0.11 Hz. These results supported the idea that the attended target was sampled rhythmically with a sampling frequency at ~1 Hz (delta frequency band).
evidence: Spectral analysis of target processing time series shown in Figure 4A supports this claim.

claim: The distractor was sampled rhythmically with a sampling frequency at approximately 1 Hz.
source: Across all participants, the averaged spectrum is shown in Figure 4Bii, where the peak frequency was determined to be 1.08±0.11 Hz. These results supported the idea that the distractor was also sampled rhythmically with a sampling frequency at ~1 Hz (delta frequency band).
evidence: Spectral analysis of distractor processing time series shown in Figure 4B supports this claim.

claim: Both the target and the distractor were sampled rhythmically at approximately 1 Hz.
source: As shown above, the present evidence suggests that both the target and the distractor were sampled rhythmically, at ~1 Hz.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the spectral analyses presented.

claim: The mean relative phase between target and distractor sampling was 0.51 ± 0.31π.
source: Figure 5A shows the distribution of the relative phase for all participants (mean relative phase = 0.51 ± 0.31π).
evidence: Phase analysis shown in Figure 5A supports this claim.

claim: The relative phase distribution between target and distractor sampling is not different from the uniform distribution.
source: A Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) test was applied to the relative phase distribution to see whether it departed from the uniform distribution (Figure 5B). A K-S statistic of 0.10 showed that the relative phase distribution is not different from the uniform distribution at p=0.92, suggesting that there was no systematic relative phase between rhythmic samplings of target vs distractor across participants.
evidence: Statistical test results support this claim.

claim: There was no systematic relative phase between rhythmic samplings of target vs distractor across participants.
source: A K-S statistic of 0.10 showed that the relative phase distribution is not different from the uniform distribution at p=0.92, suggesting that there was no systematic relative phase between rhythmic samplings of target vs distractor across participants.
evidence: This is inferred from the K-S test showing uniform distribution.

claim: If target sampling and distractor sampling are well separated in time (opposite phases), competition will be minimized and task performance will be maximized.
source: Since simultaneously presented target and distractor compete for neural representations and the stronger the competition, the worse the task performance, one may expect that if the target sampling and the distractor sampling are well separated in time, namely, if they occur in opposite phases of the 1 Hz brain oscillation, the competition will be minimized, and the task performance will be maximized.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the competition model.

claim: If target and distractor are sampled during the same phase, competition will be maximized and task performance will be minimized.
source: Conversely, if the target and the distractor were sampled during the same phase within the 1 Hz cycle, the target-distractor competition will be maximized, and the task performance will be minimized.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the competition model.

claim: In a high-performing participant, target and distractor processing time courses are highly anticorrelated with relative phase around π.
source: In the high performer, the two time courses are highly anticorrelated (relative phase is around π), indicating that the target and the distractor were sampled in opposite parts of the cycle, while for the low performer, the two time courses are highly correlated (relative phase is around 0), indicating that the target and the distractor were sampled in the same part of the cycle.
evidence: Analysis of individual participant data shown in Figure 5C supports this claim.

claim: In a low-performing participant, target and distractor processing time courses are highly correlated with relative phase around 0.
source: In the high performer, the two time courses are highly anticorrelated (relative phase is around π), indicating that the target and the distractor were sampled in opposite parts of the cycle, while for the low performer, the two time courses are highly correlated (relative phase is around 0), indicating that the target and the distractor were sampled in the same part of the cycle.
evidence: Analysis of individual participant data shown in Figure 5C supports this claim.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between relative phase and task performance (r=0.6041, p=0.0008).
source: Across all participants, as shown in Figure 5D, a significant positive correlation between relative phase and task performance was observed (r=0.6041, p=0.0008), suggesting that the more the target sampling and the distractor sampling are separated in time (i.e. in opposite phases of the cycle), the less the interference between target and distractor processing, the better the task performance.
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D supports this claim.

claim: The more target sampling and distractor sampling are separated in time, the less the interference between target and distractor processing, and the better the task performance.
source: Across all participants, as shown in Figure 5D, a significant positive correlation between relative phase and task performance was observed (r=0.6041, p=0.0008), suggesting that the more the target sampling and the distractor sampling are separated in time (i.e. in opposite phases of the cycle), the less the interference between target and distractor processing, the better the task performance.
evidence: This is inferred from the positive correlation between relative phase and performance.

claim: Both target processing and distractor processing exhibited rhythmicity at approximately 1 Hz.
source: We found that (1) both target processing and distractor processing exhibited rhythmicity at ~1 Hz and (2) the phase difference between the two rhythmic time courses was related to task performance, i.e., relative phase closer to π predicted a higher rate of coherent motion detection whereas relative phase closer to 0 predicted a lower rate of coherent motion detection.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the spectral analyses.

claim: Relative phase closer to π predicted a higher rate of coherent motion detection.
source: We found that (1) both target processing and distractor processing exhibited rhythmicity at ~1 Hz and (2) the phase difference between the two rhythmic time courses was related to task performance, i.e., relative phase closer to π predicted a higher rate of coherent motion detection whereas relative phase closer to 0 predicted a lower rate of coherent motion detection.
evidence: This is based on the correlation analysis between relative phase and performance.

claim: Relative phase closer to 0 predicted a lower rate of coherent motion detection.
source: We found that (1) both target processing and distractor processing exhibited rhythmicity at ~1 Hz and (2) the phase difference between the two rhythmic time courses was related to task performance, i.e., relative phase closer to π predicted a higher rate of coherent motion detection whereas relative phase closer to 0 predicted a lower rate of coherent motion detection.
evidence: This is based on the correlation analysis between relative phase and performance.

claim: In a target-distractor scenario, both attended and distracting information were sampled rhythmically.
source: These results suggest that (1) in a target-distractor scenario, both attended and distracting information were sampled rhythmically and (2) the more target sampling and distractor sampling were separated in time within a sampling cycle, the less distraction effects were observed, both at the neural and the behavioral level.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the spectral analyses.

claim: The more target sampling and distractor sampling were separated in time within a sampling cycle, the less distraction effects were observed at both neural and behavioral levels.
source: These results suggest that (1) in a target-distractor scenario, both attended and distracting information were sampled rhythmically and (2) the more target sampling and distractor sampling were separated in time within a sampling cycle, the less distraction effects were observed, both at the neural and the behavioral level.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the phase-performance correlation.

claim: Delta oscillations (0.5–3.5 Hz) are traditionally associated with deep sleep and homeostatic processes.
source: Delta oscillations (0.5–3.5 Hz), traditionally associated with deep sleep and homeostatic processes (Amzica and Steriade, 1998; Franken et al., 2001; Franken and Dijk, 2024; Frohlich et al., 2021; Torres-Herraez et al., 2022), are being increasingly recognized for their role in a variety of cognitive functions (Basar et al., 1999; Başar et al., 2001; Başar-Eroglu et al., 1992).
evidence: Citations support this established knowledge about delta oscillations.

claim: Delta oscillations are being increasingly recognized for their role in a variety of cognitive functions.
source: Delta oscillations (0.5–3.5 Hz), traditionally associated with deep sleep and homeostatic processes (Amzica and Steriade, 1998; Franken et al., 2001; Franken and Dijk, 2024; Frohlich et al., 2021; Torres-Herraez et al., 2022), are being increasingly recognized for their role in a variety of cognitive functions (Basar et al., 1999; Başar et al., 2001; Başar-Eroglu et al., 1992).
evidence: Citations support this emerging understanding of delta oscillations.

claim: Rhythmic sampling of an auditory scene is mediated by delta oscillations.
source: In the auditory domain, rhythmic sampling of an auditory scene is shown to be mediated by delta oscillations (Kubetschek and Kayser, 2021; Morillon et al., 2019).
evidence: Citations support this claim about delta oscillations in auditory processing.

claim: When observers directed temporal attention to one of two sequential grating targets with predictable timing, the steady-state visual evoked response was modulated at 2 Hz.
source: In a recent study, when observers directed temporal attention to one of two sequential grating targets with predictable timing, the steady-state visual evoked response of the flashing target was modulated at 2 Hz (Denison et al., 2022), which falls in the delta frequency band.
evidence: Citation supports this specific finding about 2 Hz modulation.

claim: Expecting a stimulus engages delta oscillations.
source: In addition, extensive evidence has shown that expecting a stimulus, which is known to require the deployment of attentional resources, engages delta oscillations (Arnal et al., 2011; Arnal et al., 2015; Breska and Deouell, 2017; Cravo et al., 2013; Lakatos et al., 2008; Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009; Stefanics et al., 2010).
evidence: Multiple citations support this claim about delta oscillations in expectation.

claim: Delta oscillations are involved in mechanisms that synchronize distributed regions within functional neural networks in supporting cognitive control.
source: Delta oscillations were also involved in mechanisms that synchronize distributed regions within functional neural networks in supporting cognitive control (Helfrich et al., 2017; Helfrich et al., 2019; Helfrich and Knight, 2016).
evidence: Citations support this claim about delta oscillations in cognitive control.

claim: The spatially overlapping target and distractor in the paradigm places high demand on the brain's cognitive control system, which operates in the delta frequency band.
source: The spatially overlapping target and distractor in our paradigm places high demand on the brain's cognitive control system, shown recently to be operating in the delta frequency band (Pagnotta et al., 2024), which could be another reason underlying the observed mediation by delta oscillations in the rhythmic sampling of the target-distractor environment.
evidence: Citation and inference support this claim about cognitive control demands.

claim: When two attended objects overlap in space, the relative phase between the two rhythmic behavioral time series appears to be uniformly distributed across participants.
source: When two attended objects overlap in space, however, this alternating sampling pattern is not observed, and the relative phase between the two rhythmic behavioral time series appears to be uniformly distributed across participants (Re et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation supports this claim about phase distribution with overlapping objects.

claim: Regardless of the behavioral relevance of two superimposed stimuli, there is no preferred phase relationship between their samplings at the population level.
source: Thus, regardless of the behavioral relevance of the two superimposed stimuli, there is no preferred phase relationship between their samplings at the population level.
evidence: This is inferred from the uniform phase distribution observed in the current study and prior work.

claim: The distractor decoding accuracy at the whole trial level was not correlated with task performance.
source: As shown in Figure 3D, the distractor decoding accuracy at the whole trial level was not correlated with task performance, nor was the overall power of the target evoked activity at the whole trial level.
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis supports this claim.

claim: The overall power of the target evoked activity at the whole trial level was not correlated with task performance.
source: As shown in Figure 3D, the distractor decoding accuracy at the whole trial level was not correlated with task performance, nor was the overall power of the target evoked activity at the whole trial level.
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis supports this claim.

claim: The key mechanism underlying target-distractor competition is not how well the target and distractor are each represented but how their respective rhythmic sampling aligns over time.
source: Thus, what we found should be considered a new mechanism underlying the competition between distractor and target. In this mechanism, the key is not how well the target and the distractor are each represented but how their respective rhythmic sampling aligns over time: The more target sampling and distractor sampling are separated in time, the less direct competition between the two, the better the attended information is processed, and the better the behavioral performance.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of results showing phase but not amplitude correlates with performance.

claim: When the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is high, sidebands are visible in the Fourier spectrum, whereas when the SNR is low, the sidebands are indistinguishable from the noise floor.
source: We showed using both simulations and actual data that when the SNR is high, the sidebands are visible, whereas when the SNR is low, the sidebands are indistinguishable from the noise floor (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: Simulations and data analysis shown in Appendix support this claim.

claim: The majority of subjects have low SNR for observing sidebands.
source: The majority of our subjects have low SNR for observing sidebands. This is why the sidebands in the Fourier spectrum in Figure 2B are not readily identifiable.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of SNR in the data.

claim: The 1 Hz amplitude modulation of the SSVEP amplitude and decoding accuracy time series is of an endogenous origin and represents the frequency of rhythmic sampling in the paradigm.
source: This suggests that the 1 Hz amplitude modulation of the SSVEP amplitude, as well as decoding accuracy time series, is of an endogenous origin and represents the frequency of the rhythmic sampling of the environment by the visual attention system in our paradigm.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the 1 Hz peak cannot be explained by signal processing alone.

claim: The approximately 1 Hz rhythmic sampling and the phase-related target-distractor competition are robust findings.
source: Using a 0.1 s window length and a 0.05 s step size (Appendix 1—figures 5 and 6) and applying the window-free Hilbert transform method (Appendix 1—figures 7 and 8), we found the same results as those reported in the main manuscript, suggesting that the ~1 Hz rhythmic sampling and the phase-related target-distractor competition are robust findings.
evidence: Replication with different analysis parameters supports robustness.

claim: Thirty undergraduate students from the University of Florida participated in the experiment.
source: Thirty undergraduate students from the University of Florida gave written informed consent and participated in the experiment to earn credit in an introductory psychology course.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant recruitment.

claim: Three participants were excluded due to excessive movements during recording.
source: Three participants were excluded due to excessive movements during recording.
evidence: This is a direct statement about data exclusion.

claim: The final sample consisted of 18 women and 9 men with a mean age of 19.2 ± 1.1 years.
source: The EEG data from n=27 participants (18 women, 9 men, mean age = 19.2 ± 1.1 years) were analyzed and reported here.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the final sample demographics.

claim: The RDK consisted of 175 yellow dots randomly distributed within a circular aperture.
source: The RDK consisted of 175 yellow dots randomly distributed within a circular aperture in the center of the screen, with each dot spanning <0.5 degrees of visual angle.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus properties.

claim: Each dot spanned less than 0.5 degrees of visual angle.
source: The RDK consisted of 175 yellow dots randomly distributed within a circular aperture in the center of the screen, with each dot spanning <0.5 degrees of visual angle.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus properties.

claim: The IAPS images portrayed three broad categories of emotions: pleasant, neutral, and unpleasant.
source: The IAPS images portrayed three broad categories of emotions: pleasant, neutral, and unpleasant.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus categories.

claim: The stimulus was presented on a 30-inch MR-compatible LCD monitor placed approximately 230 cm from the participant's head.
source: The stimulus was presented on a 30-inch MR-compatible LCD monitor placed approximately 230 cm from the participant's head outside the bore of the MRI scanner.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental setup.

claim: For each 4.29 Hz flicker cycle, the moving dots were displayed for 100 ms followed by a 133 ms off period.
source: For each 4.29 Hz flicker cycle, the moving dots were displayed for 100 ms, which was followed by a 133 ms off period.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus timing.

claim: For each 6 Hz flicker cycle, the IAPS background picture was shown for 100 ms followed by a 66.7 ms off period.
source: Similarly, for each 6 Hz flicker cycle, the IAPS background picture was shown for 100 ms and followed by a 66.7 ms off period.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus timing.

claim: Coherent motion instances lasted for four on-off cycles (933 ms).
source: Coherent motion instances lasted for four on-off cycles (933 ms) and appeared once in 39 trials (13 trials per emotion condition) or twice in 4 trials.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the coherent motion duration.

claim: Coherent motion instances appeared once in 39 trials or twice in 4 trials.
source: Coherent motion instances lasted for four on-off cycles (933 ms) and appeared once in 39 trials (13 trials per emotion condition) or twice in 4 trials.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: The remaining 41 trials contained no instances of coherent motion.
source: The remaining 41 trials contained no instances of coherent motion.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Each trial lasted 11.667 s (50 moving dot cycles and 70 IAPS background picture cycles).
source: Each trial lasted 11.667 s (50 moving dot cycles and 70 IAPS background picture cycles).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the trial duration.

claim: The coherent motion instances occurred in the interval between 2.3 s and 10.4 s post stimulus array onset.
source: The coherent motion instances occurred in the interval between 2.3 s and 10.4 s post stimulus array onset.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing of coherent motion.

claim: A total of 42 IAPS pictures were equally divided into three content categories based on valence: pleasant (erotic couples), neutral (workplace people), or unpleasant (bodily mutilation).
source: A total of 42 IAPS pictures were equally divided into three content categories based on valence: pleasant (erotic couples), neutral (workplace people), or unpleasant (bodily mutilation).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus set.

claim: There was a total of 84 trials: 28 pleasant trials, 28 unpleasant trials, and 28 neutral trials.
source: There was a total of 84 trials: 28 pleasant trials, 28 unpleasant trials, and 28 neutral trials, and each picture was used twice during the experiment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Each picture was used twice during the experiment.
source: There was a total of 84 trials: 28 pleasant trials, 28 unpleasant trials, and 28 neutral trials, and each picture was used twice during the experiment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: EEG data was recorded using a 32-channel MR-compatible EEG recording system.
source: EEG data was recorded using a 32-channel MR-compatible EEG recording system (Brain Products, Germany).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the recording equipment.

claim: Thirty-one Ag/AgCl electrodes were placed on the scalp according to the 10–20 system.
source: Thirty-one Ag/AgCl electrodes were placed on the scalp according to the 10–20 system via an elastic cap.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the electrode placement.

claim: Electrode FCz was used as the reference during recording.
source: Electrode FCz was used as the reference during recording.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the recording reference.

claim: EEG data was digitized at 16-bit resolution and sampled at 5 kHz.
source: EEG data was digitized at 16-bit resolution and sampled at 5 kHz with a 0.1–250 Hz (3 dB point) bandpass filter applied online (Butterworth, 18 dB/octave roll off).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data acquisition parameters.

claim: The analyzed EEG data came from the period from 2 to 11 s post array onset.
source: To minimize the transient effect resulting from the stimulus array onset and the possible effect resulting from anticipating the end of a trial, the EEG data from the beginning and the end of a trial were discarded, namely, the analyzed EEG data came from the period from 2 to 11 s post array onset, which contained the period from 2.3 to 10.4 s post stimulus array onset during which instances of coherent motion in the moving dots took place.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data analysis window.

claim: The moving window duration was 0.5 s and the step size was 0.25 s.
source: To assess target processing as a function of TFO, i.e., the temporal dynamics of target processing, the magnitude of the band-passed filtered data was obtained using a moving window approach, where the window duration was 0.5 s and the step size was 0.25 s.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the analysis parameters.

claim: The MVPA analysis was conducted with the linear support vector machine (SVM) method as implemented in the LibSVM package.
source: The MVPA analysis was conducted with the linear support vector machine (SVM) method as implemented in the LibSVM package (http://www.csie.ntu.edu.tw/~cjlin/libsvm/) (Chang and Lin, 2011).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the analysis method.

claim: The decoding process was iterated 100 times to ensure the stability of the decoding result.
source: This process was iterated 100 times to ensure the stability of the decoding result, and the average of the decoding accuracy values was analyzed and reported (Bae and Luck, 2019; Haxby et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the analysis procedure.
